title: H. G. Wells: The War of the Worlds — Ep 24/27 — "The Man on Putney Hill"
description:
He hides that night in the inn on Putney Hill, lighting no lamp for fear of the Martians. The house is stripped bare but for a crust and two tins of pineapple left by some earlier rat of a man, and he prays aloud in the dark before dawn sends him creeping out with his pockets full of biscuits.

The road is strewn with wreckage, and the common beyond it feels lonelier than ever. He stops at a marsh to watch frogs swarming stubbornly in the mud, then feels himself watched in turn: a man armed with a cutlass rises from the bushes, challenges him, and tells him of a flying-machine the Martians are learning to build. The man is an artilleryman, certain mankind is beaten and that people are now no more than ants to the invaders.

Something in the artilleryman's sweeping gesture toward London stirs the narrator, and he cries out, "Great God! But you are a man indeed!" He digs alongside him through the day, then by lamplight wins three chess games and learns poker, the two of them playing cards for the parishes of London itself.

Late that night, toasted and given a cigar, he climbs to the roof under Mars and the violet glow of the red weed, with the fires of Kensington burning beyond. The day's folly weighs on him, and he resolves to leave the dreamer behind and go on alone into London.

Chapter VII of Book Two of H. G. Wells's The War of the Worlds (1898), "The Man on Putney Hill", in the public domain.

— The Keeper's Lantern —
Every episode is one whole chapter, in order, from the first page to the last.
